note: Plain-English explanations to read out, in three levels: 'simple' (the concept in a few steps, using normal super terms such as pre-tax and after-tax), 'standard' (the rule and the key numbers, in the order a member needs them) and 'detailed' (the full rule, PDS worked examples and edge cases). Each level is an ordered list of steps: either a logic chain where every step follows from the one before, or instructions in the order they must happen. 'general' marks where general information stops and personal advice would start. Every dollar figure must exist in rates.json, the source quote, or allow_numbers (check-data.mjs enforces this). 'terms' are the phrases that get a hover-over explainer wherever they appear in a card.

items.title: Minimum annual payment
simple: A pension must pay you at least a minimum amount each financial year. It's a government rule.
The minimum is a percentage of your balance on 1 July, and the percentage rises with age.
You can take more than the minimum, but never less.
standard: The minimum is worked out once a year, on 1 July: your balance that day × the percentage factor for your age.
The factors are 4% under 65 and 5% from 65 to 74, then they keep stepping up with age.
That's the least you must be paid that financial year. You can choose more (up to 10% if it's a TTR pension).
Extra withdrawals during the year don't change that year's minimum. It's recalculated next 1 July.
In the first year it's pro-rated to the days left (see First-year pro-rata minimum).
detailed: The minimum is set once, at the start of each financial year.
It's your balance on 1 July multiplied by the age-based percentage factor for your age.
For example, at 70 with $400,000 on 1 July the factor is 5%, so the minimum is $20,000 for the year, about $1,670 a month.
Extra withdrawals during the year don't reduce that year's minimum.
In the year a pension starts, the minimum is pro-rated to the days left (see First-year pro-rata minimum).
items.general: Explain how the minimum is worked out. Don't suggest how much above the minimum to take.

source.quote: Your minimum income amount is calculated by multiplying your opening account balance by your age-based percentage factor at the start of each financial year

items.title: First-year pro-rata minimum
simple: The minimum is a yearly amount that assumes the pension runs from 1 July to 30 June.
A pension that starts part-way through the year only runs for part of it.
So in the first year, the minimum is reduced in proportion to the days left until 30 June.
standard: Start with the full-year minimum: starting balance × the factor for your age.
Count the days from your start date to 30 June, including the start date.
Multiply the full-year minimum by the days left, divide by the days in the year, and round to the nearest ten dollars.
That's your minimum for this first year. From the next 1 July it's a full-year amount on that day's balance.
If you start in June, you can choose not to be paid until the next financial year.
detailed: First work out the full-year minimum: starting balance times the age factor. At 67 with $500,000 that's 5%, so $25,000.
Then count the days left in the financial year, including the start date. A 1 October start leaves 273 of 365 days.
Round to the nearest ten dollars: $18,700 is this year's minimum.
If the pension starts between 1 June and 30 June, the member can choose to have no payment until the next financial year.
From 1 July the full-year rule applies, using the balance on that day.
items.general: Explain the calculation. Don't advise on the start date or amount.

source.quote: $25,000 (minimum amount) × 273 (days remaining in the financial year) ÷ 365 = $18,698.63

items.title: TTR compared with Retirement Phase
simple: Super is normally preserved until you retire. A TTR pension lets you draw some of it from preservation age while you're still working.
Because you're still working, a TTR pension has limits: a 10% yearly maximum, generally no lump sums, and earnings still taxed.
Once you retire or turn 65, it becomes a Retirement Phase pension and those limits fall away.
standard: A TTR pension can start from preservation age (60 for anyone born from 1 July 1964) while you keep working.
While it's TTR: payments between the minimum and 10% of your balance each year, generally no lump sums, and investment earnings taxed at up to 15%.
At 65 it converts to a Retirement Phase pension automatically. Before 65, it converts once you tell us you've retired or met another condition of release.
As a Retirement Phase pension: no maximum, lump sums allowed, and investment earnings tax-free.
detailed: TTR is an income stream you can start from preservation age while still working, with your super otherwise still preserved.
Because the money is still preserved, payments are limited to between the minimum and 10% of the balance, and lump sums generally aren't available.
Because it isn't yet in the retirement phase, earnings stay taxed at up to 15%.
It converts to a Retirement Phase Flexi Pension at 65, or once the member tells us they've met a condition of release, such as retiring or leaving a job from 60.
On conversion the maximum falls away, lump sums become available, earnings become tax-free, and the balance counts towards the transfer balance cap.
items.general: Explain the differences. Whether TTR suits someone's tax or work situation is advice: refer to UniSuper Advice.

source.quote: Once you reach age 65 or let us know you've met a condition of release allowing unrestricted access to your super (e.g. retired from the workforce or terminate employment from age 60), your TTR Flexi Pension will be converted into a Retirement Phase Flexi Pension

items.title: The TTR 10% maximum
simple: A TTR pension can pay at most 10% of its balance each financial year.
Unlike the minimum, that 10% isn't reduced when the pension starts part-way through the year.
So a late start means the full 10% is available over fewer months.
standard: The maximum is 10% of your balance on 1 July, or of your starting balance in the first year.
The minimum is pro-rated in the first year, but the maximum isn't.
So if you start late in the year, you can still take the full 10% before 30 June.
Unless you choose otherwise, it's spread evenly over the months that are left.
The maximum only applies while it's TTR. It falls away when the pension converts to Retirement Phase.
detailed: The maximum is 10% of the 1 July balance, or of the opening balance in the first year.
It isn't subject to the pro-rata rules, so a late start keeps the full 10%.
For example, a $400,000 TTR pension started in April can pay up to $40,000 before 30 June.
Spread over April, May and June, that's $13,330 a month.
Once the pension converts to Retirement Phase, there's no maximum at all.
items.general: Explain the limit. Don't suggest an amount.

source.quote: The maximum amount for TTR Flexi Pension isn't subject to the pro-rata rules.

items.title: Why money can't be added to a pension
simple: A pension starts with a single amount, and the law doesn't allow anything to be added to it afterwards.
New money, whether contributions or rollovers, goes into a super (accumulation) account instead.
From there it can start a second pension, or be combined with the first by restarting it.
standard: Once a Flexi Pension starts, nothing more can be added: it's a legal requirement.
So any new contribution or rollover goes into an accumulation account first.
You can start a second pension with it. Each pension has its own minimum and its own tax components.
Or roll the existing pension back to super, combine everything, and start one new pension. The pro-rata minimum on the old pension has to be paid first.
That's why we suggest bringing all your super together before starting, after checking you won't lose insurance elsewhere.
detailed: Once a Flexi Pension starts, no further amounts can be added: this is a legal requirement.
New money has to go into an accumulation account first.
From there it can start a new Flexi Pension, with its own minimum and its own tax components.
Some members instead roll the existing pension back to super, combine it with the new money and start one new pension; the pro-rata minimum on the old pension has to be paid before it closes.
Either way, check insurance in any fund being consolidated before moving money.
items.general: Explain the rule. Whether to consolidate first, or open a second pension, can be a personal decision.

source.quote: Once you start a Flexi Pension, you can't add further amounts to it. If you want to add money to an existing Flexi Pension account, you'll have to start a new account. This is a legal requirement.

items.title: Transfer balance cap
simple: Investment earnings in a retirement pension are tax-free, so there's a lifetime limit on how much you can move into retirement pensions.
That limit is the transfer balance cap: $2.1 million for someone starting their first retirement pension now.
It counts what you move in, not later investment growth, and the ATO keeps track of it.
standard: The transfer balance cap is a lifetime limit on how much super you can move into retirement-phase pensions, across all your funds.
For a first retirement pension now it's $2.1 million. If you started one earlier, your personal cap may be between $1.6 and $2.1 million.
What you move in counts against the cap, including a TTR pension when it converts. Lump sum withdrawals from a pension free up some cap.
Investment growth and regular pension payments don't change it.
The ATO tracks it, so your exact cap and balance are in ATO online services.
detailed: The transfer balance cap limits the total moved into retirement-phase pensions over your lifetime, and the ATO tracks it in your transfer balance account.
The general cap is $2.1 million. People who started a retirement pension earlier have a personal cap between $1.6 and $2.1 million.
Amounts moved in count against it, including a TTR pension when it converts. Lump sum withdrawals from a pension reduce what's counted; earnings and regular payments make no difference.
For example, moving $1.5 million in leaves about $600,000 of cap for future pensions, even if the first pension grows.
Going over means the ATO can require the excess to be removed, with tax on it.
The member's own cap and balance are in ATO online services.
items.general: Explain the cap. A member's own cap and options if they're near it: ATO, and advice.

source.quote: To view your transfer balance cap and your transfer balance account, please contact the ATO or log in to the ATO's online services via ato.gov.au.

items.title: Retirement Bonus
simple: In super, investment gains are taxed, so we set money aside for capital gains tax we may have to pay later.
In a Retirement Phase pension, earnings are tax-free, so some of that provision may no longer be needed.
Eligible members get it back as a Retirement Bonus when their pension starts.
standard: While money is in super, we hold a provision for future capital gains tax on its investments.
When it moves into a Retirement Phase pension, earnings become tax-free, so part of that provision may not be needed.
Eligible members receive it as a Retirement Bonus, added automatically when the pension starts. It doesn't apply to TTR.
You need 12 months' continuous membership to be eligible.
If you withdraw half or more of the pension in the first year, it may be clawed back.
detailed: The bonus passes on capital gains tax provisions that are no longer needed once assets move into the tax-free retirement phase.
It applies when a Retirement Phase Flexi Pension starts, not a TTR pension, and is added automatically.
Eligibility needs 12 months' continuous membership before the pension starts.
It may be clawed back if half or more is withdrawn in the first year.
The amount depends on the investment options and their tax provisions, so don't estimate it: refer to unisuper.com.au/retirement-bonus.
items.general: Explain eligibility. Don't estimate a specific bonus amount: refer to unisuper.com.au/retirement-bonus.

source.quote: The Retirement Bonus represents tax savings that may be passed on to eligible members when they start a Retirement Phase Flexi Pension.

items.title: Drawdown order
simple: If a pension is invested in more than one option, each payment has to come out of one or more of them.
The drawdown method sets which: Cash first (the default), an order you choose, or a share from every option (pro-rata).
The method you pick changes your investment mix over time.
standard: Default: payments come from Cash first, then the more conservative options, then growth options.
Your choice: you set the order.
Pro-rata: each payment comes from every option in proportion to its balance, so your mix stays the same.
With the default or your-choice order, the options used first run down, so the mix shifts over time.
For example, with 20% Cash and 80% Balanced, pro-rata takes each payment 20/80; the default uses the Cash first.
Which suits you is an investment decision.
detailed: Default order draws from Cash first, then progressively less conservative options.
That runs down the defensive options first, so over time the mix shifts towards growth.
Your choice order draws in the sequence the member sets, with the same kind of drift.
Pro-rata draws in proportion to the amount in each option at the time of payment, so the mix stays the same.
For example, with 20% in Cash and 80% in Balanced, pro-rata takes each payment 20% from Cash and 80% from Balanced; the default uses up the Cash first.
Which one suits is an investment decision.
items.general: Explain the methods. Which suits the member is an investment decision.

source.quote: Pro-rata – payments are drawn in proportion to the amount held in each investment option at the time of payment.

items.title: Temporary account before a pension starts
simple: When a pension application is waiting for super from other funds, the money is held in a temporary Accumulation 1 account.
It stays there, invested in Cash, until everything arrives or 90 days pass.
Then the account closes and the pension starts with the full amount.
standard: When you're rolling in super from other funds, we hold it in a temporary Accumulation 1 account.
It has no admin fees and no insurance, and it's invested in Cash so the amount stays steady.
It closes, and your pension starts, once all transfers have arrived, or 90 days after the first one, whichever comes first.
Anything arriving after that stays in super, because a pension can't be added to once it starts.
detailed: A temporary Accumulation 1 account holds rollovers and contributions while a Flexi Pension application waits for them.
It has no administration fees and no insurance, and it's invested in Cash.
It closes, and the pension begins, once all transfers are received and processed, or 90 days after the first one arrives, whichever happens first.
Amounts that arrive later stay in super, because nothing can be added to a pension once it starts.
items.general: Factual.

source.quote: The temporary Accumulation 1 account will automatically close and your Flexi Pension will begin once we've received and processed all transfers and/or contributions, or 90 days after we receive the first transfer or contribution, whichever happens first.

items.title: The $10,000 close-out
simple: A pension keeps paying until its balance falls to $10,000.
At that point the rest is paid out and the pension closes.
Where it goes depends on the type: to your bank account for Retirement Phase, back to super for TTR.
standard: Your pension continues until the balance reduces to $10,000.
Then we pay out the rest and close it.
Retirement Phase and beneficiary pensions: paid to your bank account.
TTR: rolled back to a super account, because that money is still preserved.
How long it takes to reach $10,000 depends on your balance, payments, withdrawals, returns and fees.
detailed: The pension continues until the balance reduces to $10,000.
Retirement Phase and beneficiary pensions: the remainder is paid to the nominated bank account and the pension closes.
TTR: the remainder is rolled back to an accumulation account, because the money is still preserved.
When that happens can't be worked out here: it depends on balance, payment level, withdrawals, returns and fees. Refer to the Retirement income calculator or advice.
items.general: Factual. How long a pension will last is a projection: refer to the Retirement income calculator or advice.

source.quote: Your Flexi Pension will continue until the balance reduces to $10,000

items.title: Concessional and non-concessional contributions
simple: Concessional contributions are pre-tax: employer contributions, salary sacrifice, and personal contributions you claim a tax deduction for. The fund taxes them at 15%.
Non-concessional contributions are after-tax: money you add from your take-home pay or savings without claiming a deduction. No tax going in.
Each type has its own yearly cap, and going over can mean extra tax.
standard: Ask: has this money already been taxed?
Pre-tax (concessional): employer contributions, salary sacrifice, and personal contributions you claim as a deduction. Taxed 15% in the fund, capped at $32,500 a year.
After-tax (non-concessional): personal contributions you don't claim. No contributions tax, capped at $130,000 a year.
A personal contribution starts as after-tax. Lodging a notice of intent, and getting our acknowledgement, turns it into a pre-tax contribution.
Going over either cap can mean extra tax.
detailed: Concessional: employer contributions (12%), salary sacrifice, and personal contributions claimed as a tax deduction. Taxed 15% in the fund, with Division 293 tax on top for high incomes. Cap $32,500 a year, with carry-forward if eligible.
Non-concessional: personal after-tax contributions not claimed. No contributions tax. Cap $130,000 a year, or up to $390,000 under bring-forward.
A personal contribution starts out non-concessional.
A valid notice of intent, acknowledged by us, turns it into a concessional contribution.
For example, $5,000 from savings that isn't claimed is non-concessional; lodge a notice of intent and claim it, and it's concessional.
items.general: Explain the types and caps. Whether to claim a deduction is a tax decision: suggest an accountant or advice.

source.quote: Any contributions on which you claim a tax deduction will be treated as concessional contributions

items.title: Notice of intent to claim a deduction
simple: Personal after-tax contributions can be claimed as a tax deduction, which turns them into concessional (pre-tax) contributions.
To claim, you lodge a notice of intent with us and get our acknowledgement before claiming in your tax return.
It has to happen before the money is moved, withdrawn, split or used to start a pension.
standard: Make the personal contribution.
Lodge a notice of intent online, under Manage account.
Wait for our written acknowledgement.
Then claim the deduction in your tax return. We deduct 15% contributions tax, and it counts towards the concessional cap.

Lodge the notice before your tax return and by the end of the next financial year, and before any of that money is rolled over, withdrawn, split or used to start a pension. Otherwise the deduction can't be claimed in full.
detailed: A personal contribution stays non-concessional until a valid notice of intent is lodged and acknowledged in writing.
The notice must be given before the earlier of lodging that year's tax return or the end of the next financial year.
It must also come before the contribution is rolled over, withdrawn, split to a spouse or used to start a pension; otherwise the deduction can't be claimed in full.
Once acknowledged, the amount is treated as a concessional contribution: 15% contributions tax, and it counts towards the concessional cap.
Whether to claim, and how much, is a tax question for the member's accountant.
items.general: Explain the process and timing. Whether to claim, and how much, is a tax question for the member's accountant.

source.quote: You must submit your claim (and we must acknowledge receipt in writing) before whichever of the following occurs first

items.title: Contribution splitting
simple: Contribution splitting moves some of your pre-tax (concessional) contributions into your spouse's super.
You split the previous financial year's contributions, up to 85% of them.
Your spouse must be under preservation age, or under 65 and not retired.
standard: Wait for the financial year to end: you split last year's concessional contributions.
Check your spouse can receive it: under 60, or 60 to 64 and not retired.
Work out the amount: up to 85% of last year's concessional contributions.
If you're claiming a deduction on any of it, lodge the notice of intent first.
Send the request so it reaches us by 30 June. The split amount still counts towards your concessional cap, not your spouse's.
detailed: Concessional contributions from the previous financial year can be split.
The most that can be split is the lesser of 85% of those contributions and the concessional cap.
The spouse must be under preservation age, or between preservation age and 65 and not retired.
If a deduction is being claimed, the notice of intent must be acknowledged before the split, or the deduction is lost.
For example, if $20,000 of concessional contributions went in last year, up to $17,000 can move to the spouse this year.
The request has to reach us by 30 June.
items.general: Explain eligibility. Whether splitting makes sense is advice.

source.quote: The maximum amount of contributions that can be split each financial year is the lesser of: 85% of your concessional contributions, and the concessional contributions cap applicable to you.

items.title: Carry-forward of unused cap
simple: The concessional (pre-tax) cap is $32,500 a year, and any part you don't use can be carried forward.
You can use unused cap from the past five years, as long as your total super balance was under $500,000 on the previous 30 June.
The ATO tracks how much you have available.
standard: Each year you have a concessional cap of $32,500.
Whatever you don't use is carried forward, for up to five years before it expires.
In a later year you can add those unused amounts to that year's cap, if your total super was under $500,000 on the previous 30 June.
For example, using $20,000 of a $32,500 cap leaves $12,500 to use later.
The ATO tracks the available amount, and you can see it in ATO online services.
detailed: Unused concessional cap carries forward for up to five years, then expires.
To use it in a year, total super balance must have been under $500,000 on the previous 30 June.
For example, using $20,000 of a $32,500 cap leaves $12,500 to carry forward.
The ATO works out what's available and shows it in ATO online services; we can't see it.
If the member uses it with personal contributions, the notice of intent rules still apply.
items.general: Explain the rule. The member's available amount comes from the ATO.

source.quote: Unused concessional contributions can be carried forward for up to five years, after which time they will no longer be available.

items.title: Bring-forward of the after-tax cap
simple: The non-concessional (after-tax) cap is $130,000 a year.
If you're under 75, you can bring forward up to two future years' caps and contribute up to $390,000 at once.
Doing that uses up those future years' caps.
standard: The usual after-tax cap is $130,000 a year.
If you're under 75, going over it starts a bring-forward period: you can use up to three years' caps at once, $390,000.
Those future years' caps are then used up for the rest of the period.
How much you can bring forward depends on your total super balance on the previous 30 June. At $2.1 million or more, the after-tax cap is nil.
detailed: Going over $130,000 of non-concessional contributions in a year, while under 75, starts a bring-forward period.
Total super balance on the previous 30 June decides whether it's a two- or three-year period, and how much can go in.
The full three years allows $390,000. At $2.1 million or more, the non-concessional cap is nil.
Once the period starts, its total is fixed for that period.
For example, someone with $800,000 who sells an investment could put in $390,000 this year, then nothing more after tax for the next two years.
Using it is a planning decision: refer to advice.
items.general: Explain the rule. Using it is a planning decision: refer to advice.

source.quote: The cap amount you can bring forward, and whether you have a two or three-year bring-forward period, will depend on your total super balance at the end of June of the previous financial year.

items.title: Preservation age and conditions of release
simple: Super is preserved: you generally can't access it until you reach your preservation age and meet a condition of release.
Preservation age is 60 for anyone born from 1 July 1964.
The main conditions are retiring, leaving a job after 60, or turning 65.
standard: Your preservation age is between 55 and 60 depending on your date of birth, and 60 for anyone born from 1 July 1964.
Once you've reached it, you can access your super if you retire.
From 60, ending a job also releases it, even if you work again later.
At 65 you can access it whether you're working or not.
Before that, only limited exceptions apply: severe financial hardship, compassionate grounds, terminal illness, or a TTR pension from preservation age.
detailed: Access needs two things: preservation age, and a condition of release.
Preservation age is 55 to 60 by date of birth, and 60 for anyone born on or after 1 July 1964.
The main conditions are retiring after preservation age, ending a job from 60, or turning 65.
Others include severe financial hardship, compassionate grounds and a terminal medical condition.
A TTR pension gives limited access from preservation age while still working.
For example, someone born in 1966 can access super after retiring at 60 or later, or at 65 regardless.
items.general: Factual. Whether someone has 'retired' for super purposes can depend on their circumstances: check the rules.

source.quote: Generally, you must keep your super in the super system until you permanently retire from the workforce on or after reaching your preservation age

items.title: Taxable and tax-free components
simple: Your super has two components: tax-free (mostly your after-tax contributions) and taxable (pre-tax contributions and earnings).
Every withdrawal takes from both in the same proportion. You can't choose.
From 60, withdrawals are tax-free, so the components mainly matter under 60 and for death benefits.
standard: Tax-free component: mostly non-concessional (after-tax) contributions.
Taxable component: employer contributions, salary sacrifice, deducted personal contributions and earnings.
Every withdrawal includes both in the same proportions as your whole balance. If 10% is tax-free, a $10,000 withdrawal is $1,000 tax-free and $9,000 taxable.
Under 60, only the taxable part can be taxed. From 60, withdrawals are tax-free.
The components still matter for a death benefit paid to someone who isn't a tax dependant.
detailed: Every benefit has a tax-free component and a taxable component.
Any lump sum must include both components in the same proportions as the whole benefit.
For example, if 10% of the balance is tax-free, a $10,000 withdrawal under 60 is $1,000 tax-free and $9,000 taxable.
Only the taxable component can be taxed, and only under 60; from 60, withdrawals are tax-free.
Components still matter for death benefits to non-dependants: up to 17% on the taxed element.
The member's actual components are on their statement.
items.general: Explain the components. The member's actual components are on their statement.

source.quote: Any lump sum withdrawal you make must include taxable and tax-free components in the same proportions as your entire benefit.

items.title: Binding, non-binding and reversionary nominations
simple: Super doesn't automatically form part of your estate, so you nominate who should receive it if you die.
A binding nomination must be followed by the Trustee. A non-binding one is a preference the Trustee considers.
A reversionary nomination applies to pensions: payments continue to that person instead of a lump sum being paid.
standard: Super isn't automatically covered by your will, so a nomination tells the Trustee who should receive it.
Binding: if it's valid when you die, the Trustee must pay the people you named, in your proportions.
Non-binding: the Trustee considers it, but decides.
Reversionary (pensions only): your pension keeps paying to that person, and it overrides any other nomination on that pension.
You can only nominate dependants (spouse, children, financial dependants, interdependents) or your estate.
detailed: Without a nomination, the Trustee decides how to pay among dependants and the legal personal representative.
A binding nomination, lapsing or non-lapsing, must be followed if it's valid and in effect at death: a lump sum in the nominated proportions.
A non-binding nomination guides the Trustee's decision but doesn't bind it.
A reversionary nomination (Flexi Pension, not BIS) keeps the income going to that person, overrides any other nomination on that pension, and can't be split.
Only dependants or the legal personal representative can be nominated; who counts as a dependant for tax is narrower.
items.general: Explain the options. Which one suits someone's family and tax situation is advice.

source.quote: If the nomination is valid and still in effect at the date of your death, the Trustee must pay your account balance as a lump sum to the beneficiaries in the proportions you've nominated.

items.title: Lapsing and non-lapsing binding nominations
simple: Binding nominations come in two kinds: non-lapsing, which lasts until you change it, and lapsing, which expires after three years.
Non-lapsing can be done online. Lapsing needs a paper form signed in front of two witnesses.
An expired lapsing nomination is treated as non-binding.
standard: Non-lapsing: lodge online or on paper. It stays in place until you change or revoke it.
Lapsing: paper form only, signed in front of two adult witnesses who aren't beneficiaries.
A lapsing nomination expires three years after you signed, last changed or last confirmed it.
To renew it, send us a signed and dated written confirmation before it expires.
If it expires or is invalid, it's treated as non-binding. A paper form with no type ticked is lapsing.
detailed: Both kinds need: only dependants or the legal personal representative, exactly 100% allocated, and signed by the member, not a power of attorney.
Non-lapsing: online or paper. It doesn't expire; it stays until amended or revoked.
Lapsing: paper only, witnessed by two people aged 18 or over who aren't beneficiaries. It lasts three years from signing, last amendment or confirmation.
To renew, the member sends a written notice, signed and dated, before it expires. This is the member's responsibility.
An expired or invalid nomination is treated as non-binding. A paper form with no type chosen defaults to lapsing.
items.general: Factual.

source.quote: A valid binding death nomination (non-lapsing) won't expire unless you amend or revoke it, so it doesn't need to be confirmed or updated every three years.

items.title: When default cover starts
simple: Accumulation 1 members get default Death and TPD cover automatically, without health questions.
It starts once you're 25 and your balance reaches $6,000, with your employer's next contribution.
You can opt out before it starts so no premiums are charged.
standard: Two conditions: you're 25 or older, and your balance is at least $6,000.
Once both are met, 10 units of Death and TPD cover start with the next employer contribution, with no health questions.
That contribution has to arrive within 180 days, or the cover won't start.
If you don't want it, opt out before it starts, so no premiums are deducted.
If you're under 25 or under $6,000, you can still apply within 180 days of starting with an eligible employer, without health evidence.
detailed: Default cover in Accumulation 1 needs age 25 or over and a balance of at least $6,000.
Once both are met, cover starts on the date the next employer contribution is received, as long as it's within 180 days.
Default is 10 units of Death and TPD without health evidence, with Income Protection where it applies.
Members under 25 or under $6,000 can apply for cover within 180 days of starting with an eligible employer, without health evidence.
Opting out before the start date means no premiums are deducted.
For example, someone who turns 25 in March with $7,000 would see cover start with their next pay's contribution.
items.general: Explain when cover starts. Whether to keep, change or cancel cover is the member's decision.

source.quote: Your Death and/or TPD cover (including any top-up cover) and Income Protection cover will start on the date we next receive an employer contribution into your Accumulation 1 account after you're aged 25 and have an account balance of at least $6,000

items.title: Why unitised cover goes down with age
simple: Unitised cover is bought in units, and the cost per unit stays roughly the same.
The amount each unit pays out depends on your age: it peaks in your late 30s, then falls.
So with the same number of units, your cover goes down as you get older.
standard: With unitised cover you hold a set number of units at a roughly steady cost per unit.
Each unit's cover amount depends on your age: it peaks at $27,500 at 38 and falls after that.
So the same units give less cover as you age. For example, 10 units are worth $266,000 at 35 but $86,000 at 55.
To keep a steady cover amount, you can convert to fixed cover. Then the premium rises with age instead.
detailed: Unitised cover: the number of units is fixed, the cost per unit is roughly level, and the cover per unit depends on age.
Cover per unit peaks at $27,500 for death and TPD at age 38, then falls.
For example, 10 units are worth $266,000 at 35 but $86,000 at 55.
Fixed cover keeps the amount steady and the premium rises with age instead.
Which suits is a personal decision.
items.general: Explain how it works. Whether unitised or fixed suits someone is a personal decision.

items.title: Inactive accounts and insurance
simple: An account is inactive if it hasn't received a contribution or rollover for 16 months in a row.
Insurance on an inactive account stops, unless you've told us you want to keep it.
If an inactive account is also under $6,000, it may be transferred to the ATO.
standard: Count the months since the last contribution or rollover.
At 16 consecutive months with none, insurance stops, unless you've elected to keep it.
If the balance is also under $6,000, the account may have to be transferred to the ATO.
The ATO then tries to consolidate it into another active super account in your name.
These are legal rules to stop small, forgotten accounts being eroded by fees and premiums.
detailed: Inactive means no contribution or rollover for 16 consecutive months.
At that point insurance ends, unless the member elected to keep it before then.
Inactive accounts under $6,000 are transferred to the ATO unless an exception applies.
The ATO consolidates them into an active account where it can.
For example, if contributions stopped in January 2026, cover would stop around May 2027 unless the member had asked to keep it.
Keeping cover is the member's decision.
items.general: Factual. Whether to keep cover is the member's decision.
